synthesis.brief_result: Twenty startups joined the list in this first run, led by AQEMIA, a French company that designs new medicines with physics and AI. The strongest newcomers build machines and molecules again: Maven Robotics' warehouse robot, Kepler Aerospace's satellite swarm and EveryCarbon's plastics made from waste. The trend of the week is AI agents that take over a professional's paperwork, from patents and insurance files to hiring and bookkeeping.
gaps_result: Jack & Jill put an AI agent on both sides of hiring and Zero replaced the sales CRM. Nobody on the list has built the same two-sided agent for the other big matching markets: finding a doctor, a tradesperson or a tenant.
AQEMIA and EveryCarbon pair physics and biology with AI to design medicines and plastics. The same recipe is missing for food and fertiliser, where farmers need new molecules just as badly.
Stream and Thatch reach millions of hourly workers by selling through the employer. No one uses that channel yet for what those workers struggle with next: rent deposits, childcare or legal help.

Kepler Aerospace and Maven Robotics build hardware for governments and warehouses. No entry brings cheap robots or satellite data to smallholder farms in Asia or Africa, where BuuPass shows the phones are already in everyone's pocket.

Tarabut and Insurely built consented financial-data pipes for the Gulf and the Nordics. Latin America and Southeast Asia, where Ontop and Bumame operate, still lack that layer, and whoever builds it will own the region's fintech back end.

weeks/2026-09-16-r1.json.brief: Twenty startups joined the list in this first run, led by AQEMIA, a French company that designs new medicines with physics and AI. The strongest newcomers build machines and molecules again: Maven Robotics' warehouse robot, Kepler Aerospace's satellite swarm and EveryCarbon's plastics made from waste. The trend of the week is AI agents that take over a professional's paperwork, from patents and insurance files to hiring and bookkeeping.
gaps: Jack & Jill put an AI agent on both sides of hiring and Zero replaced the sales CRM. Nobody on the list has built the same two-sided agent for the other big matching markets: finding a doctor, a tradesperson or a tenant.
AQEMIA and EveryCarbon pair physics and biology with AI to design medicines and plastics. The same recipe is missing for food and fertiliser, where farmers need new molecules just as badly.
Stream and Thatch reach millions of hourly workers by selling through the employer. No one uses that channel yet for what those workers struggle with next: rent deposits, childcare or legal help.

Kepler Aerospace and Maven Robotics build hardware for governments and warehouses. No entry brings cheap robots or satellite data to smallholder farms in Asia or Africa, where BuuPass shows the phones are already in everyone's pocket.

Tarabut and Insurely built consented financial-data pipes for the Gulf and the Nordics. Latin America and Southeast Asia, where Ontop and Bumame operate, still lack that layer, and whoever builds it will own the region's fintech back end.

weeks/2026-09-16-r2.json.brief: This week's list grew to 50 startups, with 31 joining for the first time. The strongest newcomer is Ayar Labs, an optical chip startup that raised $650 million this year to fix a data-movement bottleneck slowing down AI data centers. The trend of the week is private space infrastructure, as newcomers like The Exploration Company and MBRYONICS build the capsules, rockets and laser communication hardware that let governments and companies run their own space missions.
gaps: AI medical scribes like Nabla, Tandem Health and Voize all target doctors and nurses; nobody here builds the same speak-instead-of-type note automation for vets, dentists or mental health therapists, professions with the same paperwork burden and much less competition.

Space hardware builders like The Exploration Company, MBRYONICS, Kepler Aerospace and Open Cosmos are multiplying, but nobody insures the satellites and missions they launch; a Stoïk-style insurer built specifically for space assets and mission failure could pair naturally with this wave.

Cross-border fintechs like barq, Aspora, Ontop and Stream serve migrants, expats and gig workers, but none of them serve refugees or asylum seekers, who have similar cross-border money needs plus no credit history and often no bank account at all.

AI-for-science startups like AQEMIA, Cradle and Cubase Bio apply generative AI and physics to drugs and proteins; the same approach could be pointed at breeding new crop varieties faster, a natural extension for a company like xFarm that already has farm-level data but no molecular design layer.

trends.name: AI legal tech
trends.sentence: A wave of startups are using AI to help lawyers and companies research law, draft documents, review contracts and manage legal work faster.

trends.name: AI shortcuts lab science
trends.sentence: Several startups pair generative AI with physics or biology simulation to design new drugs, proteins, materials or engineering products without years of trial-and-error lab work.

trends.name: Cross-border finance for underserved workers
trends.sentence: Fintechs are building banking, payroll and payment products specifically for migrants, expats, gig workers and hourly employees who traditional banks ignore.

trends.name: Private space infrastructure
trends.sentence: Startups are building the hardware for satellites, launch vehicles and optical communications that let governments and companies run their own space missions.

trends.name: AI medical scribes
trends.sentence: AI tools that listen to doctor-patient conversations and automatically write structured clinical notes are appearing across multiple countries to cut clinician paperwork.

trends.name: Cybersecurity gets specific
trends.sentence: Security startups are moving away from broad vulnerability scanning toward embedded, developer-first or exploitability-focused defenses that tell teams exactly what to fix.

weeks/2026-09-21-r3.json.brief: This week the hot startups list grew to 50 companies, with 22 new names joining for the first time. The strongest newcomer is Lovable, a Swedish startup that lets anyone describe an app in plain English and have its AI write the code and put it online, turning a technical breakthrough into something any ordinary person can use. The trend of the week is AI agents that do the work, not just chat, as startups like Lovable, Factory, n8n and Yoom sell agents that carry out whole jobs end to end instead of just answering questions.
gaps: Latin America is nearly invisible in this batch, with only Ontop (Colombia) representing the whole region through global payroll; nobody is pointing the molecule/material-design playbook of AQEMIA, Cradle and CuspAI, or the clinical-documentation playbook of Nabla and Tandem Health, at Latin America's huge agriculture or healthcare markets.

Elder care has no entry at all, even though Evvy shows a founder can win by targeting an underinvested health niche and Maven Robotics shows a wheeled arm-robot can be built for one ugly job; nobody has built the equivalent AI monitoring, companionship or robotics product for aging-in-place seniors.

Skilled trades and independent tradespeople (electricians, plumbers, HVAC techs) are only touched at the edges, through FYLD's construction field-data capture and Sona/Stream's frontline-worker pay tools; nobody offers the direct matching-and-dispatch layer that Jack & Jill built for white-collar job seekers or Maven Robotics built for warehouse labor.

Everyday mental health support is a gap: Loora proves people will hold real practice conversations with an AI tutor, and ElevenLabs/Synthflow show voice agents are now trusted for sales and tutoring calls, but nobody in this list has aimed that same conversational-voice technology at day-to-day mental health coaching or therapy support.

Sub-Saharan Africa is missing from the fintech and health-diagnostics wave; the MEA entries (barq in Saudi Arabia, Tarabut in Bahrain, Zeal in Egypt) cluster around the Gulf and North Africa, leaving open the same regulated-wallet or at-home-diagnostics model (as Evvy runs for women's health) for markets like Nigeria or Kenya.

trends.sentence: Space startups are building the physical backbone of the sector, from reusable capsules and laser comms terminals to small and swarm satellites, sold mainly to governments and commercial operators.

trends.name: Self-fixing security and compliance
trends.sentence: Security and compliance tools are moving from just flagging problems to acting on their own, patching vulnerabilities, blocking attacks and running audits automatically.
